messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

After the high‑speed collision, Amir, a 30‑year‑old tax inspector, was inundated with images of shattered glass and the screech of tires. The scent of gasoline and a black sedan parked nearby jolted him. To avoid confronting the flashbacks, he began scrolling his phone, playing games, and surfing the internet—screen escape. When meals passed, he ate barely enough, another way to numb the pain. He also refused to drive, opting for a rideshare to work. Each honk or sudden noise in his office would set Amir’s heart racing, as if a crash were imminent. The unexpected sounds triggered a high‑alert state, making him hypervigilant and causing him to jump at ordinary noises. These threat reactions echoed the crash imagery, the alcohol smell, and the sight of similar cars that haunted his every step. Amir’s conviction that he could no longer rely on himself, that he had become incapable of the work that defined him, and that his emotions were forever muted, fed into his coping. Believing he was powerless, he avoided eating, convinced he would starve if he tried to maintain routine. He also turned to his phone, thinking it shielded him from overwhelming incompetence. His negative appraisal therefore drove the very strategies he had adopted. The conviction that he could not rely on himself made Amir’s threat response even more intense. He was perpetually on guard, ready to react to any danger, even if the threat was simply a passing breeze. This heightened state of hypervigilance amplified his startle to ordinary sounds, and his constant alertness amplified the feeling that the world was an ever‑present battlefield. Because Amir felt he could not rely on his own judgment, he began noticing triggers everywhere. Every car passing the courthouse, every faint scent of alcohol in the cafeteria, every image of damaged vehicles in the news reminded him of the day he felt powerless. His self‑deprecating beliefs made him hyper‑attuned to potential danger, so he reported more triggers than before. Amir’s elevated threat state sharpened his perception of trigger cues. While walking through the city, the echo of a distant horn would set his mind racing with the memory of the crash, and he would immediately think of similar cars he had seen on the highway. Hypervigilance turned every ordinary sound into a possible reminder, pulling the triggers back into the foreground of his consciousness. By retreating to screens and cutting back on food, Amir reinforced his belief that he could not trust himself. Each hour spent scrolling only deepened his sense of isolation, and the lack of nourishment made him feel physically weak. His maladaptive strategies, in turn, solidified the negative appraisal that he had lost the capacity to manage life’s demands. Meanwhile, the more Amir spent time on his phone and the fewer meals he ate, the more his threat response grew. Isolation and hunger intensified his hypervigilance, and the constant mental gymnastics left him drained at the end of the day. He now finds himself unable to concentrate on filing taxes, fearing the loss of his job and the purpose it once gave him. The escalating cycle finally pushed him to seek therapy, hoping to break free and reclaim safety and competence.
